Published in final edited form as: Subst Use Addctn J. 2025 May 5;46(3):757–782. doi: 10.1177/29767342251326374 Abstract Background: Cocaine use disorder (CUD) is a significant and insufficiently studied public health issue, especially considering that the global prevalence of CUD is estimated to be higher than ever. There is still no consensus on effective treatments for CUD. Important barriers for research in the field include the high attrition levels observed in randomized controlled trials (RCTs) for CUD treatment and the lack of emphasis on methods to reduce attrition in CUD RCTs. Methods: The goal of this study was to systematically review over 2 decades of CUD RCTs, with the objective of evaluating the reporting of attrition bias and methods used to mitigate attrition. Results: Our scoping review extracted information from 106 RCTs, of which only 82 explicitly evaluated attrition as an outcome. Thirty-eight studies had an attrition rate above 50%, and five 16 studies had medium attrition bias, 6% to 19%. The remaining 68 had large attrition bias. Conclusion: Across all included studies, discussion of attrition as a limitation was uncommon. Overall, these analyses suggest that most RCTs evaluating CUD treatments have not adequately accounted for attrition in their analyses or employed approaches to mitigate attrition. Keywords: drug abuse, attrition rate, cocaine, imputation techniques, dropout, cocaine user disorder, randomized clinical trials, missing data, attrition bias Introduction While much attention has been drawn to opioid and amphetamine use disorders in recent years, cocaine use disorder (CUD) remains one of the most common and fastest-growing substance use disorders (SUDs) worldwide. In the United States, cocaine-related overdoses have been found to have mortality rates as high as those opioid-related overdoses, particularly in minoritized patient groups.1 In South America, Brazil has the highest CUD-related disease burden globally, with its 2019 per 100 000 rates nearly doubling its 1990 rate.2 Worldwide, cocaine manufacturing is estimated to be at its highest level ever.3 Relative to opioids and amphetamines, CUD remains an understudied public health problem worldwide, even though cocaine-related problems are as likely to result in hospital admission as opioid-related problems.4 Despite many years of effort, no Food and Drug Administration pharmacologic treatments were approved for CUD.5 To date, there remains a limited consensus on medications or psychotherapies deemed to be effective in reducing cocaine use, promoting abstinence, and avoiding relapses among people with CUD. Throughout the past 40 years, many medications have been studied, with different levels of success, but until now none of them has proven its efficacy. Dopamine agonists and antagonists, antidepressants, anticonvulsants, prescription psychostimulants, naltrexone, among others have already been tested.6 CUD trials have historically struggled with low attrition rates, which adds heavy bias to the trials’ results.6 A major limitation in research concerning treatment for CUD is the inadequate understanding of the factors related to the attrition rate, whose extent can be as high as 80% on the treatment of CUD and its impact on patients’ outcomes.7 Broadly speaking, the estimated effectiveness of SUD treatments is often biased by treatment discontinuation, a significant obstacle to assessing whether the results of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) can be generalized to the real-world.8 In clinical settings, research from several other SUDs (not CUD) has indicated that treatment discontinuation is often the norm rather than the exception. For instance, an analysis of real-world administrative data in an outpatient addiction treatment facility in Brazil found an attrition rate of 82% from November 1997 to April 2014, with a median treatment duration of 15 days.9 In an American sample of patients receiving pharmacological treatment for opioid use disorder, 64% were discontinued treatment before 6 months of initiation.10 The co-occurrence of other SUDs together with CUD was also found to exacerbate attrition rates.11 These high attrition rates in real-world settings raise important questions about the significance of treatment discontinuations and whether CUD RCTs are factoring attrition into their study designs and manuscript discussion sections. It is known that attrition can introduce bias if the characteristics of participants with missing data differ between the randomized groups. For instance, ineffective treatment may appear ostensibly effective if subjects with a more severe burden of illness discontinue their assigned treatment.11 High attrition rates may hinder the external validity of RCT data, especially if attrition is not explicitly discussed in the limitations section of RCTs. A vivid example of the severe impact of study attrition on RCTs in addiction science can be seen in12 the X: BOT trial, which compared extended-release naltrexone (XR-NTX) to buprenorphine-naloxone (BUP-NX) for opioid relapse prevention. Although the study considered both drugs to be equally effective toward relapse-free survival and overdose reduction, what ostensibly appears to be equipoise XR-NTX and BUP-NX, this conclusion is complicated by the high treatment discontinuation rates associated with XR-NTX. fetched_contents.text: Strategies for participant retention in long term clinical trials: A participant –centric approaches Abstract A clinical trial is the most foolproof method to evaluate the efficacy of a new intervention. Successful completion of clinical trials depends on the retention of the participants enrolled. Poor participant retention can lead to significant time and cost burden and have potentially adverse biases on the results. A high retention rate of participants is an important criterion for the validity and credibility of randomized controlled clinical trials. Many long-term trials fail due to low retention of study participants. Efforts at participant retention should start even before the first participant is recruited into the study. Retention is not only the responsibility of the investigators but also all other stakeholders in a clinical trial. In recent years, retention materials, participant camps, and introduction of national study coordinators have helped in improving retention. Quality of the relationship developed between the research staff and the study participant is a key factor for success of any trial. In our experience, in the context of resource-challenged low- and middle-income countries, we have found that it is possible to achieve high retention rates, 95%–100%. The rapport built between the investigating team and the participant plays a vital role in retention. In addition, personalized care, including listening to the participant's problems and enabling to contact investigators or study team at any time of the day, has shown benefits in retention. Keywords: Clinical trials, retention, stakeholders INTRODUCTION The randomized clinical trial is the most scientific method to access the effectiveness of treatment.[1] The success of a clinical trial depends on the ability to recruit participants in a systematic manner, to ensure adherence to and integrity of intervention, and to retain the participants through the entire study duration and follow-up. Power of the study will be affected if the retention rate is poor, and selection bias is introduced.[2] The reliability of results and validity of the study are affected by poor retention.[3] Successful recruitment and retention of participants is the most challenging aspect in the conduct of clinical trials.[4] Participant selection is crucial for retention. Retention is a continuous process, and plans for retention strategies should start during protocol development and from the onset of recruitment. Therefore, it is essential to understand effective retention strategies, as participant retention is a major practical challenge – often the “Achilles Heel” of trials – especially in resource-constrained situations, as in low- and middle-income countries. There are many challenges in achieving high retention, which include lack of trust, socioeconomic barriers, inconveniences, real or perceived adverse events from intervention, migration of the subject from the study site, personal reasons, and influence of media.[5] Complexity of the study, nature of disease studied, need to take time off from work, education and occupation level, and interference from physicians not involved in the study and family members are other factors to be considered.[6] At times, retention remains a challenge even if recruitment is successful. Recent data between the years 2000 and 2006 examining trends in recruitment and retention showed that recruitment dropped by 16% whereas retention dropped by 21%.[7] Studies have shown an 88% dropout due to the following reasons – lost to follow-up, nonadherence to protocol, and withdrawal of consent.[8] On the other hand, multiple strategies which include the presence of a study team that is respectful and supportive of participants during the entire study period, developing a good relationship with the participant, access to the investigators at any time of the day, and meticulous monitoring and corrective action on an ongoing basis, when all these are well employed, can help enhance retention.[9] In some cases, provision of additional investigations related to clinical needs other than the trial investigations may also help in retention.[10] CHALLENGES IN RETENTION Retention and recruitment are interlinked. When the duration of the study becomes long and the number of study visits increase, it becomes an added burden to the participants and to the study team.[11] This factor needs to be considered during the design of the study, and strategies put in place to ensure unbiased recruitment and high retention. On average, 25%–26% of the participants drop out after expressing their consent.[12,13] More than 90% of the studies are delayed due to failed enrollment or challenges to participant retention, which includes loss of participants to follow-up.[14] In a survey assessing the challenges in participant retention, it was found that 44% of the participants feared side effects. Fear of study procedures and change of residence were reported by 47% as the reasons for dropping. Lack of support from the family physician and family members was reported by 27%, while 55% of the participants stated that the lack of dedicated approach by an investigator's team and 9% each reported negative media publicity and perceived lack of efficacy of the treatment as reasons for dropping out.[4] Other retention challenges include inconvenient location, schedule conflicts, perception that the disease condition is not improving, lack of appreciation for their participation, and unrealistic expectations from the treatment. fetched_contents.text: Efficacy of acupuncture for cocaine dependence: a systematic review & meta-analysis Abstract Background Acupuncture is a commonly used treatment option for the treatment of addictions such as alcohol, nicotine and drug dependence. We systematically reviewed and meta-analyzed the randomized controlled trials of acupuncture for the treatment of cocaine addiction. Methods Two reviewers independently searched 10 databases. Unpublished studies were sought using Clinicaltrials.gov, the UK National Research Register and contacting content experts. Eligible studies enrolled patients with the diagnosis of cocaine dependence of any duration or severity randomly allocated to either acupuncture or sham or other control. fetched_contents.text: Initial treatment dropout in patients with substance use disorders attending a tertiary care de-addiction centre in north India Abstract Background & objectives: Dropout from substance use disorders treatment is associated with poor outcomes. Although many factors have been associated with an early dropout of patients, the reasons for dropping out of treatment prematurely remain poorly understood particularly in the Indian context. This study was aimed to study socio-demographic and clinical variables predicting initial dropout of patients attending a tertiary care de-addiction treatment centre in north India. Methods: Information was extracted from the records of consecutive newly registered patients from January 2011 to December 2014. The patients who did not come for follow up within 30 days of the first contact were defined as initial dropouts. Results: Data of 7991 patients could be retrieved. Majority of the sample consisted of male, married and employed individuals. Of them, 4907 patients (61.3%) were considered initial dropouts. Multivariate analysis revealed that after controlling for other factors, greater age, being employed, lower educational status, lesser duration of substance use, use of alcohol, opiate, tobacco, cannabis or sedative-hypnotic use but the absence of multi-substance use predicted initial drop out. Interpretation & conclusions: This study identified some socio-demographic and clinical variables which might predict treatment attrition in substance use disorders. Clinician's awareness towards these factors and tailor-made intervention might improve initial treatment retention. Future research could be directed to find the validity of this assumption. Keywords: Alcohol, de-addiction, dropout, opioids, retention, substance use disorder ---------------------------------------- Long-term retention of a patient in any treatment programme is known to be associated with a positive outcome. Moos and Moos1 have demonstrated that initial treatment entry and retention can predict long-term outcome in alcohol dependence, even at the end of 16 yr. Another naturalistic study on mixed substance use disorder population has demonstrated a dose-response relation between duration of treatment and outcome2. Treatment retention in substance use disorder programmes has also been effective in reducing criminal behaviour, improving the state of health, engaging in gainful employment and overall better outcome3. Hence, retaining the individual with substance use disorders in the treatment net constitutes an important goal of treatment. Yet, it is remarkable that high dropout rates are encountered in the substance use treatment settings4,5. It has been suggested that highest rates of dropouts occur in the initial stages of treatment and can be as high as 50 per cent in the first month of treatment6,7,8. The predictors of attrition from de-addiction treatment setting vary across the studies. A positive association between immediate dropout and male gender, history of mental illness in the family and addiction to alcohol combined with other illicit substance has been shown6. Pre-treatment cocaine use, weak therapeutic alliance with counsellors, secure attachment style and better-coping strategies were associated with shorter retention9. Furthermore, younger age, greater cognitive dysfunction, maladaptive personality functioning, more drug use, lower severity of alcohol dependence and highly controlling treatment environment were found to be associated with dropout10,11. A study examining the outpatient sample has found that early dropout was associated with less education, female gender, cocaine as the primary drug and being referred from outside the larger medical centre12. Early age of onset of substance abuse and polydrug abuse are associated with higher risk for early dropout from both in- and out-patient settings13,14,15. Further, client-related factors, such as lower perception of treatment benefits16, depression and avoidance coping17 and lack of social support18 have been shown to relate to higher dropouts. Although many factors have been shown to be related to early dropout, the reasons for clients dropping out of treatment prematurely remain poorly understood in view of inconsistent findings. The lack of uniform agreement in defining dropout/completion between the studies further adds to this inconsistency. Identifying clients at risk for early dropout may help in focused attempts to increase retention in treatment programme, thereby improving the outcome. The findings of two Indian studies on treatment non-completers in de-addiction setting19,20 are limited by the fact that they included only opioid-dependent subjects and were carried within the inpatient setting specifically, hence curtailing the generalizability of results. Studies focusing on substance use disorders at the outpatient setting and including a wide variety of substance use disorders are lacking. Hence, this study was conducted to examine the socio-demographic and clinical variables that predict initial dropout of patients attending a de-addiction outpatient in north India. Branch report on enrollment barriers specific to cocaine-dependent patients

Common eligibility criteria and how they exclude or deter participants  
Cocaine-dependence trials often impose strict eligibility criteria that can exclude or deter participants. The evidence here is strongest for cocaine use disorder (CUD) trials more broadly, not just acupuncture studies, but it still highlights a recurring theme: trial design and outcome reporting are often insufficiently mature, with attrition rates as high as 80% in some CUD studies and many trials failing to explicitly evaluate attrition as an outcome [N1-F1]. For acupuncture trials specifically, a systematic review and meta-analysis found that most trials were hampered by large loss to follow-up, which weakens the strength of inference [N3-F3]. This implies that trial eligibility and retention are often designed in a way that does not fully account for the practical realities of enrollment and ongoing participation. The same review also notes that inclusion criteria excluded trials with polysubstance use or dependence [N3-F3], which is relevant because cocaine-dependent patients may have comorbidities that make them ineligible or less likely to enroll.

Stigma, mistrust, and accessibility issues in recruitment  
The evidence base points to a broader problem of stigma and mistrust in addiction research, even though the provided material is not cocaine-specific. The CUD scoping review states that cocaine-related problems are as likely to result in hospital admission as opioid-related problems, but CUD remains an understudied public health problem [N1-F1]. It also notes that attrition bias and methods to reduce attrition are inadequately addressed in CUD RCTs [N1-F1]. A separate source on substance use disorder dropout in India found that early dropout was associated with factors such as lower educational status, being employed, lesser duration of substance use, use of alcohol, opiate, tobacco, cannabis, or sedative-hypnotic use, but the absence of multi-substance use predicted initial dropout [N5-F4]. This suggests that patients may be reluctant to enroll if they fear stigma, feel their condition is not recognized as treatable, or believe they are too burdened to participate. The recruitment and screening processes for outpatient cocaine trials were also explicitly evaluated in one source, indicating that recruitment mechanisms themselves can create barriers [N1-R3].

How trial location, timing, and burden affect willingness to enroll  
Trial location, timing, and burden are repeatedly highlighted as retention and recruitment challenges. The CUD scoping review reports that attrition is common in randomized controlled trials and that high attrition rates may hinder external validity [N1-F1]. In a resource-constrained context, participant retention is described as “a major practical challenge,” with the relationship between the research staff and participant being key to success [N2-F2]. The same source notes that retention challenges include inconvenient location, schedule conflicts, perception that the disease condition is not improving, lack of appreciation for participation, and unrealistic expectations from the treatment [N2-F2]. A review of substance use disorder dropout also found that treatment severity and comorbidities were associated with dropout [N5-F4], which means that cocaine-dependent patients may be especially deterred by trial burden if the intervention is time-consuming, requires frequent visits, or demands lifestyle changes. The evidence also suggests that socioeconomic barriers, lack of trust, migration, and perceived adverse events from the intervention can prevent enrollment [N2-F2]. For acupuncture trials, the feasibility issue is further compounded by the need for acupuncture delivery, which may add logistical burden compared with simpler interventions [N3-F3].

Overall, enrollment barriers in cocaine-dependent patients are shaped by strict eligibility criteria, stigma and mistrust, and practical burdens such as location, timing, and the overall trial burden. These factors are not confined to one trial design; they are reinforced across CUD and addiction-trial literature [N1-F1][N5-F4][N2-F2][N3-F3].

Reasons participants discontinue or drop out of trials  
The evidence is consistent that dropout is common and often multifactorial. The CUD scoping review notes that attrition rates can be as high as 80% in some studies and that discussion of attrition as a limitation is uncommon [N1-F1]. It also states that attrition can introduce bias if participants with missing data differ between randomized groups, and that high attrition may reduce external validity [N1-F1]. In a broader clinical-trials context, the evidence says that 25%–26% of participants drop out after expressing consent, and over 90% of studies are delayed due to failed enrollment or retention challenges [N2-F2]. A source on why patients drop out of clinical trials lists reasons such as financial burden, time and scheduling conflicts, lack of understanding and engagement, travel burden, anxiety and emotional concerns, and adverse event fears [N5-R5]. A substance-use-disorder dropout study found that early dropout was associated with lower educational status, being employed, lesser duration of substance use, use of alcohol, opiate, tobacco, cannabis, or sedative-hypnotic use, but absence of multi-substance use predicted initial dropout [N5-F4]. This means that dropout is not simply a matter of apathy; it is often driven by competing life demands, perceived burden, and individual risk profiles.

How treatment severity and comorbidities affect retention  
Treatment severity and comorbidities are clearly linked to retention. The CUD scoping review emphasizes that attrition is a major limitation in CUD RCTs and that treatment discontinuation is often the norm rather than the exception [N1-F1]. It also notes that co-occurrence of other SUDs together with CUD exacerbates attrition rates [N1-F1]. In the broader substance-use-disorder dropout literature, early dropout was associated with lower educational status, being employed, lesser duration of substance use, and use of other substances, while absence of multi-substance use predicted initial dropout [N5-F4]. Another source found that immediate dropout was associated with male gender, history of mental illness in the family, addiction to alcohol combined with other illicit substances, and lower perceived treatment benefits [N5-F4]. This suggests that patients with more severe symptoms, greater comorbidity, or less perceived benefit are especially vulnerable to discontinuation. The CUD scoping review also notes that attrition rates are high in real-world settings, including an outpatient addiction treatment facility in Brazil where 82% of patients attrited within 15 days [N1-F1], which reinforces the idea that retention is especially difficult in severe or complex cases.

Role of motivation, expectancy, and therapy engagement in retention  
Motivation, expectancy, and therapy engagement are central to retention. The substance-use-disorder dropout study found that lower perception of treatment benefits was associated with dropout [N5-F4]. It also found that pre-treatment cocaine use, weak therapeutic alliance with counsellors, secure attachment style, and better coping strategies were associated with shorter retention [N5-F4]. A separate source notes that poor patient engagement in clinical trials drives costly dropouts [N2-R5], and that participant rapport, personalized care, listening to participant problems, and enabling contact with the study team all help retention [N2-F2]. The same source emphasizes that retention is a continuous process and that plans should start during protocol development and from the onset of recruitment [N2-F2]. In other words, retention depends not just on the intervention itself, but on how the trial is designed, how participants are engaged, and how the research relationship is built [N2-F2][N5-F4]. The evidence is therefore not only that patients drop out because of burden, but also because they are not sufficiently motivated, do not expect the intervention to help, or do not feel engaged with the therapy.

Overall, retention barriers in addiction treatment trials are driven by high attrition rates, competing life demands, treatment severity and comorbidities, and weak motivation or engagement. The evidence supports a view that dropout is a complex, multifactorial process rather than a single failure of willpower [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F4][N5-R5].

How trial duration, frequency, and follow-up affect retention  
Trial duration, frequency, and follow-up are major retention determinants. The CUD scoping review reports that attrition rates can be as high as 80% and that discussion of attrition as a limitation is uncommon [N1-F1]. It also notes that attrition can introduce bias and may hinder external validity [N1-F1]. In the broader clinical-trials context, the evidence states that retention challenges include inconvenient location, schedule conflicts, perception that the disease condition is not improving, lack of appreciation for participation, and unrealistic expectations from the treatment [N2-F2]. It also notes that when the study duration becomes long and the number of study visits increases, it becomes an added burden to participants and to the study team [N2-F2]. A separate source says that over 90% of studies are delayed due to failed enrollment or challenges to participant retention [N2-F2]. This implies that frequent visits, prolonged follow-up, and complex schedules increase the practical burden on participants and make retention harder. The evidence also says that retention is a continuous process that should start during protocol development and from the onset of recruitment [N2-F2], reinforcing that trial design must anticipate and mitigate retention issues rather than treating them as afterthoughts.

Role of comparator arms, blinding, and control conditions  
Comparator arms, blinding, and control conditions are important methodological features, though the evidence here is more general than acupuncture-specific. The CUD scoping review emphasizes that attrition bias and methods to reduce attrition are inadequately addressed in CUD RCTs [N1-F1]. It also notes that missing data can cause bias if participants with missing data differ between randomized groups [N1-F1]. A broader clinical-trials source states that poor participant retention can lead to significant time and cost burden and adverse biases on results [N2-F2]. In the acupuncture context, the systematic review and meta-analysis found that most trials were hampered by large loss to follow-up and that the strength of inference was therefore weakened [N3-F3]. While the evidence does not provide a direct acupuncture-specific comparator arm review, it does show that methodological quality matters for interpretation. The acupuncture review also notes that the authors sought to identify methodological issues in controlled evaluation of acupuncture [N3-R3], and that reporting quality was assessed for randomization procedure, allocation concealment, blinding of patients, care providers, outcome assessors, and adequate description of loss to follow-up [N3-F3]. This indicates that blinding, adequate reporting of comparator arms, and attention to follow-up are important to reduce bias and improve trial validity.

How setting and clinician-patient relationships influence participation  
Setting and clinician-patient relationships are strongly implicated in participation. The CUD scoping review reports that attrition is a major limitation in CUD RCTs and that high attrition may hinder external validity [N1-F1]. In the broader clinical-trials context, the evidence states that retention is a continuous process and that rapport built between the investigating team and participant is a key factor for success [N2-F2]. It also notes that personalized care, listening to participant problems, and enabling contact with the study team at any time help retention [N2-F2]. A substance-use-disorder dropout study found that weak therapeutic alliance with counsellors was associated with shorter retention [N5-F4]. This suggests that participation is not only affected by the trial’s logistics but also by the interpersonal environment: if clinicians are disrespectful, unapproachable, or not responsive, patients are less likely to stay enrolled. The evidence also mentions that retention materials, participant camps, and national study coordinators can help improve retention [N2-F2], indicating that the trial setting and its support structures are part of the retention mechanism.

Overall, methodological and contextual factors are central to retention. Long duration, frequent visits, and prolonged follow-up increase burden and dropout risk [N2-F2][N1-F1]. Comparator arms, blinding, and control conditions are important because they affect bias and interpretation, especially when loss to follow-up is large [N1-F1][N3-F3]. Setting and clinician-patient relationships matter because rapport, support, and responsiveness can improve participation [N2-F2][N5-F4]. In short, retention depends as much on the trial design as on the treatment itself.

Acceptability and perceived efficacy of acupuncture among patients  
Acceptability and perceived efficacy are important acupuncture-specific challenges. The evidence shows that acupuncture is often framed as an alternative or adjunct treatment for addiction, including cocaine dependence, but its acceptance can be variable. The systematic review and meta-analysis concluded that acupuncture does not support the use of acupuncture for cocaine dependence and that most trials were hampered by large loss to follow-up [N3-F3]. Another review states that there is currently no evidence that auricular acupuncture is effective for cocaine dependence and that the evidence is not of high quality [N6-R3]. A separate source notes that some clinical reports and uncontrolled studies have suggested auricular acupuncture may be efficacious for cocaine addiction, but that this is not supported by the systematic review and meta-analysis [N3-R4]. The acupuncture review also states that the authors conclude there is no evidence that any form of auricular acupuncture is effective for cocaine dependence and recommend better studies [N6-R5]. This mixed picture suggests that patients may have varying beliefs about acupuncture, but the evidence does not support a strong consensus that it is widely accepted or effective in cocaine dependence trials.

Feasibility of acupuncture delivery in trial settings  
Feasibility is a major issue in acupuncture trials. The acupuncture review explicitly discusses methodological issues that arise in the controlled evaluation of acupuncture [N3-R3]. The systematic review and meta-analysis states that most trials were hampered by large loss to follow-up and that the strength of inference was weakened [N3-F3]. In the acupuncture-specific evidence, the trial design is also complicated by the need to randomize patients with cocaine dependence, define appropriate control conditions, and manage loss to follow-up [N3-F3]. The acupuncture review also notes that authors contacted 5 authors to identify additional published or unpublished studies and to clarify methodological issues [N3-F3], indicating that trial design and execution are not straightforward. The evidence further suggests that acupuncture delivery may be less feasible than simpler interventions because it requires specialized personnel, standardized treatment protocols, and careful monitoring of adverse events and follow-up [N3-F3]. These factors can make acupuncture trials more burdensome to conduct than other treatment studies.

Potential confounding factors and outcome measurement issues  
Confounding and outcome measurement are important limitations. The systematic review and meta-analysis found that the pooled odds ratio estimating acupuncture’s effect on cocaine abstinence was 0.76 (95% CI, 0.45 to 1.27), which is not statistically significant, and that most trials were hampered by large loss to follow-up [N3-F3]. It also states that the strength of inference is weakened by large loss to follow-up [N3-F3]. The acupuncture review notes that the authors abstracted data on study methodology and outcomes, pooled studies providing biochemical confirmation of cocaine abstinence, and assessed reporting quality [N3-F3]. The evidence also indicates that reporting quality was assessed for randomization procedure, allocation concealment, blinding of patients, care providers, and outcome assessors, and that adequate description of loss to follow-up was part of methodological reporting [N3-F3]. This implies that outcome measurement issues can arise from insufficiently rigorous methods, incomplete follow-up, and inadequate blinding. In addition, the evidence shows that trials may include different comparator arms, which can complicate interpretation [N3-F3]. Overall, acupuncture trials for cocaine dependence face confounding from loss to follow-up, variable comparator arms, and methodological weaknesses that can obscure true treatment effects.
